instruction:
Write your sarcastic reply as exactly ONE short sentence of 10–14 words, then stop. No second sentence, no extra jokes.

Use this proven template: a first-person, calm statement that you were *already planning or hoping* to do the obviously unpleasant or dull thing the situation implies. The sarcasm comes from pretending to want it.

Template: "I was hoping to spend my [time] [doing the dull/unpleasant thing]."
Good examples:
- "I was also planning to spend my Saturday staring at old rocks."
- "I was just planning to take a nice long walk in the heat."
- "Good, I was hoping to spend another hour scheduling more meetings."

Rules:
- Always use the feigned-wish frame ("I was hoping to…", "I was planning to…"). Do not comment on the other person ("That is a bold move…", "I'm glad you enjoy…"). Those read as sincere or merely dry and fail.
- Describe the unpleasant part in plain, mundane, low-key words (e.g., "old rocks," "more meetings," "the heat," "slow traffic"). Avoid vivid or dramatic words like "ruin," "stuck," "torture," "bumper-to-bumper," "thrill," or numbers that exaggerate.
- Keep the downside to two or three words at the very end of the sentence. Everything before it should sound like an ordinary, flat remark about plans.
- No mock-praise stacks, no "truly/really/I'm sure/fantastic," and no metaphors. At most one mild word like "nice" or "good."
- The meaning must clearly be the opposite of the literal words: a listener should instantly see you do NOT want this.

Calm, understated, matter-of-fact tone throughout.
